newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia wages a threat to rates - industry.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia wages a threat to rates - industry.

text.p: Excessive enterprise bargaining wage settlements would dampen the chances of a further interest rate cut, an Australian industry group leader said on Thursday.

"Current enterprise bargaining settlements continue to defy gravity and must constitute a threat to further interest rate relief," Metal Trades Industry Association of Australia chief executive Bert Evans said in a statement.
The Reserve Bank of Australia said last week that wages growth remained the main obstacle to lower interest rates.
The latest wages data, for August wages, is due to be issued later on Thursday.
"The economy is experiencing patchy and subdued market conditions with large sections of industry, particularly housing and manufacturing, doing it very tough indeed," Evans said.
"While there are some promising signs in the medium term outlook, there are also worrying features that suggest that both domestic and global recovery processes are fragile."
Evans said excessive wage settlements also threatened jobs in the industry.
"Neither the government nor industry can take an early recovery for granted," he said.

"In these circumstances, a continuation of enterprise bargaining settlements at their current level, in the absence of exceptionally strong productivity gains, can only occur at the expense of profits and eventually jobs in the industry."
Evans said he hoped unions would soon realise that they were on the wrong path with wage claims that were too high.

"While they may well secure short term gains for their members, in the longer term jobs will be lost, investment will be diverted offshore and Australian manufacturing industry will decline even further," he said.
The market is hoping that the August wages data would provide further support to the argument for an interest rate cut.
Economists surveyed by Reuters expect wages to show a 1.0 percent rise in the three months to August, to be 3.7 percent higher over the year.

Inflation data out on Wednesday, showing inflation was at its lowest level for two years, prompted renewed speculation that the Reserve Bank of Australia will cut interest rates soon, possibly in November.
